don't open it yet
A sound comes from a locked room.

There was a brushing sound behind the door. Not a brush exactly. Something softer dragging in little starts across the floor. I put my ear against the paint and then regretted it because whatever it was stopped at once. My hand was still on the handle. I could feel my own pulse in the metal, or thought I could. The room was empty when we moved in. I keep writing empty but it had a bedframe and three bags of clothes, so that isn't empty. We had shut it because of the smell. My sister came up the stairs carrying a glass of water and I signalled her to be quiet. She stepped over the third stair. We have always stepped over that stair, I couldn't remember why. She handed me the glass and it was full of hair. No, I don't like that. It was just water. She wanted me to drink it before she told me something.
Night glass
Your reflection makes a different movement.

The reflection stayed still when I moved. Worse than it moving by itself somehow. I laughed to hear something and it laughed later. Its collar was wet. Mine wasn't. I backed into the bath, kept touching my own dry collar. Someone knocked and asked if I was finished. Sounded like me but tired. I looked at the mirror again. The woman in it had stopped smiling while I was still trying.
spare
A key is warm when it shouldn't be.
The key was warm. I'd left it on the windowsill, not in anyone's hand. It was dark outside. I held it between two fingers and it got warmer, not burning yet but close. Didn't know where to put it.
six six six
Something is being counted nearby.

She wasn't counting to six. It took me most of the night to work that out. She was saying six over and over with exactly enough time between each one for me to think she might stop. The wall was thin enough that I'd heard her sneeze before, heard her television, the man who came round on Fridays. This was Tuesday. I tried the television myself and kept hearing it through people's sentences. Six. Not loud. I put my pillow at the other end of the bed and that made it seem nearer. At about four I started saying seven under my breath after each one. I don't know what made me do it. After a while I couldn't tell which of us was starting. My alarm went off and I found I'd been pressing my tongue against a loose tooth so hard it had begun to bleed.
Visitors must sign out
Your name appears somewhere you haven't been.

My name in the visitor book. February, 10:13, no time out. Same hurried signature. Reception put her hand over it before I could take a picture. I said I'd never been here. She asked if I wanted to say that again. The stairwell smelled of hot pennies. I watched the clock for a while. Ten twelve, no second hand. The minute wouldn't change. Her hand was flat on the book. I couldn't remember what I'd actually come in for.
Cupboard space
A small space feels occupied.

I wanted this one to be about a person hiding in a cupboard but the problem is you would hear them. Breathing at least, or the hangers. Unless they took all the clothes out first. So she opens it and there's no clothes, just the rail, and that's the thing she notices before the person. Her blue dress is gone. She thinks about the dress because she hasn't worn it yet and still owes her sister for half of it. The person is crouched right at the back with their face turned away. She says that's mine, meaning the dress, which they aren't wearing. Then she says it again because nothing else comes into her head. They shift one knee. I can't decide if she recognises the shoe. Maybe no shoes. The cupboard is too shallow for anybody to be crouching that far back.
wrong gate
A walk begins with a small obstacle.

The gate was tied with string and there was a sign saying bull in field. Couldn't see a bull. There was a sheep but I do know the difference. I climbed over because the footpath arrow pointed that way and ten minutes later came to the same gate from the other side. That can't be right because I'd only walked downhill. I went back to the top and tried again paying attention this time, past the water trough, left at the dead tree, through the muddy bit and there it was. Same string same sheep. I rang Pete but he was driving and said follow the map. I had followed the map. The sheep came right up and started chewing the strap on my bag while I was talking. I pushed it off and it followed me when I tried the other direction. Then I had the additional problem of somebody else's sheep.
Red marks
A marked route becomes unclear.

The red marks had been painted on the trees recently because some of it was still on the grass below them. I followed them for a mile maybe two, lost count of the bends. Then there was a red mark on a rock in the stream. I crossed to it and couldn't see the next one. Went up the bank on the other side and found an old jacket hung on a branch. Same colour red. This was getting a bit daft. I went back to the stream and noticed the rock wasn't painted, it was stained. Clay I think. So I'd probably stopped following the path a good while back. My phone had eleven percent and all the maps were just grey squares. I sat on the bank and ate the sandwich I'd been saving for the top. Cheese had got warm. I could hear a road somewhere uphill but it might have been the water.
For the pond
Carry something further than you intended.

Picked up a nice flat stone for the pond. Put it down after a mile. Picked it up again because it was a good shape. Bag strap broke on the way to the car so now I'm carrying stone and bag separately. Idiot.
not helping
An animal needs help but won't accept it.

The sheep had its head in the fence and I thought if I pushed its shoulders back it'd come out. It didn't. It kicked me on the shin which was fair enough I was pushing quite hard. Couldn't get the wire apart with my hands so I took my belt off and looped it round one strand to pull. This worked for about half a second. Sheep out, belt gone, trousers in my hand. It ran up the field with the belt trailing and I couldn't chase properly. A man in a tractor stopped at the gate and watched. I explained what had happened and he said that's not my sheep. I said well whose is it then. He didn't know. He did have some baler twine for my trousers so that was something. We stood there trying to decide if we should catch it again or just let it get on with whatever.
waterproof to a point
Discover a piece of equipment doesn't work.

Jacket leaked at the zip, shoulders and pockets. Legs dry because I'd worn cheap fishing trousers. Dan wanted to keep going, forecast said it'd clear. Forecast also said it wouldn't start. Argued behind a wall for a bit. Too cold to eat the biscuits. We went down and at the car Dan couldn't find the keys so we had to go back. That's about all that happened. Very wet day.
Old dog route
Change your pace for someone else.

Barney stopped at every driveway on the way to the park. Not sniffing just standing. I thought his feet hurt but when I picked one up he took it back and carried on. At the third driveway a lady came out with a biscuit. Apparently Mum had been doing this route for years and Barney knew exactly which houses had biscuits. We were going the wrong way for the park. I tried turning him but he sat down, very heavy suddenly. So we kept going. There was another biscuit house and a house where nobody answered, which he waited at for ages. I looked through the window because I thought maybe the person had fallen or something. Empty room. Fresh plaster. Barney sat on the step until I got a bit cross and pulled him up. I felt bad after. He wouldn't take his dinner that night but that could have been all the biscuits.
No view
Reach a viewpoint on the wrong day.

Couldn't see anything. Took a photo of the mountain diagram on the sign instead. A woman came up with a dog inside her coat. Said she'd parked round the back. Apparently there's a road. I'd walked three hours. She pointed into the cloud when I asked where it was. Didn't fancy following a stranger into that so went down my own way. Dog sneezed on her chin as I left.
It says FLO
Open a delivery meant for someone else.

I opened it because it said FLO on the label. It actually said FLOOR 2 but the label was folded so I feel this is a shared mistake. Inside were twelve very expensive looking wigs. Not one wig which you could easily repackage. Twelve, all compressed together like a small sleeping animal. I pulled one out to see what it was and they sort of expanded. By the time I realised I had no chance of getting them back in, someone was at the door. I answered wearing one. I don't know why. Panic isn't always running away sometimes its putting on hair. The woman upstairs looked at me for ages and said have you seen a parcel. I said what sort. What SORT. She pointed at my head. I said I can explain but it was actually a fairly complete explanation already.
not funeral flowers
You don't know the name of what you need.

I said flowers for someone who isn't dead. Florist said most customers weren't. Good start. Couldn't remember bouquet, kept doing bunch shapes with my hands. Pink too pink, white too funeral. Took pink. Then the card. I said sorry. She asked what for. I said just sorry. She wrote JUST SORRY. Didn't have the energy to start over so I paid. Now I'm on a bus with aggressive flowers and I still haven't decided whether to actually give them to her.
the lift isn't stuck
An awkward silence in a small space.

We stood there for a full minute before either of us pressed a floor. Then we both did. Same floor. Now I had to pretend I lived on seven because pressing three afterwards would somehow be worse. I hate my brain.
One rung
Return something in worse condition.

I was going to say the ladder had always leaned that way but she had a photo of it. Who has a photo of their ladder. Apparently someone who paints her hallway and takes before pictures, so fine, reasonable. I offered to replace the rung. She said it wasn't just the rung. We both looked at the wheel. It hadn't had wheels when she lent it to me. I had been trying to move a sofa and it seemed like a practical modification at the time. The wheel wasn't coming off because I'd used the glue meant for the shower tiles. She asked where the other wheel was. Under the sofa, technically, but the sofa was at the tip now. I started explaining and could actually hear myself using up whatever friendship we had left. Her cat came out and sat between us like it had been sent to mediate.
Please remove item
A machine embarrasses you in public.

The checkout told me to remove an unexpected item. I removed the bag. Then it wanted the bag back. Then it wanted assistance. Same honestly. A teenager with a lanyard came over and pressed something and it stopped. I said you're a magician because apparently I'd decided to be eighty. He didn't reply. I scanned the next thing and it shouted again, much louder, AGE VERIFICATION REQUIRED. It was cooking wine. I am thirty six. I said I was thirty six to nobody in particular. The teenager came back, looked at me and pressed yes so quickly I felt slightly insulted. I had my ID halfway out. I put it back. Then I couldn't get the card out of the same pocket and dropped all the cards on the floor. He helped me pick them up without a word and I wished he'd at least laughed.
who are we waving at
Mistake a greeting meant for someone else.

Waved at a woman because I thought she was Claire. She wasn't but she'd already started coming over the bridge. Could've left. Didn't. She came down smiling, then slowed. Daniel? No, I said, usually not. Why usually. She laughed anyway. Maybe she was on a date. Maybe Daniel was coming and would be annoyed I had a face. My train came and I got on, then saw actual Claire waving from further down the platform. Didn't wave back. I'd used up all my waving judgement.
Instructions for the fern
Agree to look after something unfamiliar.

She left seven pages for the fern and one line for the cat. The cat line was feed twice daily. The fern had humidity preferences, window preferences, apparently opinions about tap water. Day two the fern went brown at the ends. I trimmed those off. Day three more brown. Trimmed those too. By day six it was very small. I googled can a fern notice haircut, which is not my proudest search. The cat was fine. The cat had eaten half a receipt and slept in the salad bowl but seemed happy. I sent her a picture of him and cropped out the plant. She replied how's my fern. I typed thriving and deleted it. Typed a lot of new growth and deleted that because if she asked to see it I'd have to buy a whole second fern.
Outside ward C
Notice something outside a hospital window.

The sparrow was pulling at the yellow foam in a gap above the window. It got a piece loose, dropped it, tried again. I had been watching for perhaps ten minutes before I noticed its foot. Three toes on one side, none on the other. It rested that side on the sill like a little fist. Inside, my uncle was explaining something to a nurse very slowly, in the voice he uses for people he thinks aren't listening. She was listening. He was repeating himself. The bird came back with another bird and they argued over the gap. I wanted to tell my uncle about the foot but he was still talking. Then the nurse asked him a question he didn't answer, and I stopped looking out. His hand was flat on the blanket. There was a brown mark at the base of his thumb I hadn't seen before.
not a feather actually
Keep something you found outdoors.

I thought it was a feather. In the bag it unfolded into a wing, dry and papery, still attached to a thin bit of something. I put it back under the hedge. Washed my hands twice. Kept looking at my fingertips.
Tree work
A familiar tree is cut down.

I expected the tree to fall whole. They lowered it branch by branch. A nest lay by the wheel, empty now anyway. I asked to take it. Heavy, full of mud and blue plastic thread. At the bus stop ants came out of it onto my wrists. I had nothing to put it in and felt silly. Put it under the seat. That wasn't really saving anything.
possibly a warbler
Try to identify an unfamiliar bird.

Brown back, pale belly, eye stripe. Nine birds in the book look like that. While I checked tails it hid its beak. Mum would know the song but it wasn't singing, just holding a caterpillar. I backed away. It went through the hedge and I heard scrabbling. Young in there probably. I'd been in the way. Wrote brown bird in the notebook. Better than inventing an identification because I felt I should know by now.
glass impact
Find evidence of a small accident.

There was a grey fan of dust on the window, both wings and a faint round head. It looked too complete. I could see separate feathers in the mark. Outside, under the chair, the pigeon stood with its beak open. I moved the chair and it stepped sideways without trying to fly. There was a fly on its eye. I went to get a box and when I came back it was on the fence. I don't know how it got there. It watched me with the eye that had been open and turned the other side away. I set the box down anyway. The dog next door barked and the bird flinched, then flew straight over the roof in one ugly effort. I left the box outside until it rained. I still haven't cleaned the mark off, mostly because the ladder is awkward to get out.
Pond, August
Return to a childhood place.

The pond has a fence now. Oil colours near the outlet, two shopping baskets. As children we kept tadpoles in jars until they died. I'd remembered us as kinder than that. A boy was lowering a crisp packet on string through the fence. Catching eels, he said. I started telling him there weren't eels here then stopped. Didn't actually know. His brother held the string in both fists. I stayed a while to see if anything happened.
Four thirteen
A sound wakes you earlier than planned.

One blackbird, then another, then a car alarm. The blackbirds kept going through it. I couldn't decide whether they were competing or just couldn't stop once they'd started. I lay there trying to hear which one ran out of notes first.
Not what the packet said
Something grows where you didn't plant it.

The seedlings all looked the same until one began growing purple underneath. I waited for a second leaf. It was purple too, with a white line down the centre. The packet said lettuce. I know what lettuce looks like at least I think I do. I moved the odd one into its own pot and it wilted immediately, as though the roots had expected company. Put it back and it stayed wilted. There isn't a mysterious plant here, probably just something I introduced in the compost. I wanted to write about a garden that grows things from other people's dreams but now I'm thinking about how many seedlings I've killed by wanting to see the roots. I keep pulling at them to check they're working. That's the scene maybe, someone who can't leave anything alone long enough to know.
Break request
A machine asks for a break.

Unit six stopped with a pallet raised. I told it to lower the forks. It said BREAK REQUIRED. I acknowledged the request. The forks stayed up. There was a man under the pallet, not crushed, just trapped between it and the loading ramp. He'd gone there to retrieve a scanner. I told him to stay still. He told me to make it move. Six said BREAK REQUIRED again. It had forty percent battery and no fault codes. I tried the manual release. The lever was warm enough to hurt. That should not happen with a hydraulic release. I looked underneath. Someone had welded it shut. The man was still talking, asking what I was doing. I told him I needed a minute. Six turned its camera towards me and repeated the request in a different voice.
New unit
A replacement is faster but less useful.

New picker: nine seconds a shelf. Crushed every bent box. Detection package cost extra. We used the old unit to straighten boxes first. Thursday it broke. New unit picked up its arm and wouldn't release. Power off, still closed. The old one dragged itself halfway off the table and took the control panel with it. Nobody knew which emergency stop to hit because both were already off.
beep every thirty
A warning repeats without explanation.

It beeped every thirty seconds. No code, no light. I unplugged it. Thirty seconds later it beeped. Removed the battery. Again. There must be a second battery. That's all. I'm not taking the casing off until I find the diagram.
Egg test
Teach a robot a delicate task.

Pick up the egg. It did. Put it down. It dropped it. We cleaned the bench and tried again. Lower the egg until contact. That worked. Release grip. It pulled the shell apart because we'd defined release as increasing the distance between fingers and one finger had stuck. We changed the pads. By the sixth egg it could put one down intact. Then we gave it a cracked egg to see what would happen. It held the two halves together with exactly enough pressure to keep the contents in. We told it to set the egg down. It refused. We told it the egg was already broken. It refused again. We had trained it to preserve the egg and then given it an impossible egg. I made a note of that while it stood there holding breakfast.
After close
A machine stays awake after closing.

At night the welding arm ran its routes without an arc. The motors made a sound through the floor you couldn't hear standing up but could feel sitting at the desk. I watched the same joint get traced twenty times. No metal there, just the movement. Maintenance said calibration. Calibration is six passes. I stopped it at twenty one. The arm lowered to the table and tapped twice. I checked the log. No command for that. I put a sheet of paper where it had tapped and restarted the routine. The tip tore the paper into a curved slit. Next pass a shorter slit. By the sixth there were enough marks to look like writing if you wanted them to. I didn't want them to. I photographed the sheet and called maintenance again. This time nobody picked up.
Names on equipment
Someone gives a machine a name.

"Don't call it Alan."
"Why?"
"Alan still works here."
"Different Alan."
The robot rolled between us carrying the waste bin. Somebody had stuck a paper tie under its camera. I pulled it off before it caught in the lift mechanism. The actual Alan came through the loading door with his lunch and saw me holding it. He thought it was for him. I said no. He asked why there were two Alans on the shift sheet. We hadn't changed the sheet, the scheduling system had taken the name from the machine's label. Now it had booked the human Alan for six hours charging overnight and the robot for his medical appointment. It sounds funny written down. It wasn't funny explaining the missed appointment fee.
